report:
Your proposed answer—“no”—is not supported. The better conclusion is: EMDR can reduce PTSD symptoms for many adults, though it is not uniquely superior and should be delivered by a trained clinician.

Cochrane’s review of psychological therapies for chronic PTSD found individual trauma-focused CBT, EMDR and non-trauma-focused CBT were similarly effective immediately after treatment (https://www.cochrane.org/th/evidence/CD003388_psychological-therapies-chronic-post-traumatic-stress-disorder-ptsd-adults). A later meta-analysis comparing EMDR with CBT found both reduced PTSD/anxiety/depression symptoms, with no clear consistent advantage (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9778888/). Major guidelines therefore list EMDR among evidence-based trauma-focused options: APA describes EMDR as a PTSD treatment option (https://www.apa.org/ptsd-guideline/treatments/eye-movement-reprocessing), and VA/DoD materials summarize recommended trauma-focused psychotherapies for PTSD (https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/txessentials/overview_therapy.asp).

Caveats: effects vary by trauma type, comorbidity, therapist competence and study quality; EMDR is not a guaranteed cure, and whether eye movements themselves add benefit beyond exposure/therapeutic factors remains debated. So the evidence supports “yes, often helpful,” not “no.”
